Fossils discovered on N2

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
A huge treasure trove of fossils, including of some species that have not been documented by scientists before, has been discovered during construction work on the N2 highway near Grahamstown. Dr Robert Gess a palaeontologist who does consulting for Sanral said the discovery was significant because "many species have not yet been documented by palaeontologists". The fossils are from the the Devonian era which lasted from about 416 million years ago to 354 million years ago, and is often referred to as the "Age of Fishes". The earth at that stage was made up of only two large continents. South Africa was part of one of those called Gondwana, nearly 360 million years ago.

He said between 20 and 30 types of fossil land plants, waterweeds and seaweeds have been collected from the rocks retrieved from roadworks at Waterloo Farm, and are being described by scientists. Some of the remains from Waterloo Farm include fragments of scorpions which represent the earliest known remains of land living creatures from the ancient supercontinent of Gondwana.

Sanral is now planning to turn the area into a stop and rest area for motorists.

We plan to film Dr Gess on site and driving to the site. Perhaps speak to one of the construction workers and also SANRAL environmental manager Mpati Makoa who will talk about how they are going to turn this area into a stop and go tourist site to preserve the fossils. We can get access to the film that SANRAL made and the insert can be complimented hopefully by magnificent graphics showing the continents moving.

I do think we can make this quite an exciting piece.

Press Release:


N2 Fossil Find
A treasure trove of fossils, including species never before documented, has been unearthed by construction workers on the N2 highway near Grahamstown. Carte Blanche digs up the dirt on these unique findings.


Script:



The planet as we know it - but it has changed form and shape over hundreds of millions of years. This is a representation of the Devonian period from 420 million to 359 million years ago when the earth was made up of two super continents. To put that into perspective it predates dinosaurs by 120 miilion years.

This location just outside grahamstown where fossil discoveries are being made was once an estuary in the Devonian age. Where we were standing here was just 15 degrees from the South Pole. Which means South Africa was much further south than it current position, and Grahamstown was in the antarctic circle.

Rob: There is something quite miraculous about the fact that within the rocks we have a record of the history of the planet and by interpreting the rocks we can understand how the continents have moved and reconfigured and how life and the history of life have entirely changed and evolved.

Palaeontologist and lecturer Dr. Robert Gess, is one of SA's foremost expers on Devonian fossils. He is a research fellow and is based at the Albany Museym in Grahamstown. Unlike most motorists, he is unperturbed about the delays caused by road works on the N2 . These delays are a small price to pay, he believs because they have allowed for the discovery of never before documented fossils from the Devonian age.

LINK: To the untrained eye they look like ordinary roadworks but these round green hills conceal secrets about the world hundreds of millions of years old and it is only when new roads are developed that their secrets are revealed. This section of the road was last worked on 150 years ago.


On the 1st of June SANRAL announced that as a result of controlled rock blasting, at this site called Coombs Hill, a treasure trove of fossils had been unearthed.

Rob: So it is only when they have road works they cut through a hill. It allows us to reach right down into the hill and bring out really fresh rock from inside the hill.

And that same process unfolded 23 years ago at a differeit site known as waterlook farm which is 20 kilmeteres from new site at coombs Hill. In 1989 a new road had been cut into the hills just a kilometer from Grahamstown. Between 1993 and 1995, Dr. Gess was part of a team that began excavations. A fossilized time capsule was found, the first of its type in the entire world.

John: Doctor what is it about waterloo farm that makes it so significant?
Rob: Well before waterloo farm was found we didn’t have a single site of this age in the world which came from a high latitude that’s near the pole sort of circumstance because 360 million years ago where we are was 15 degrees from the south pole so actually in the Antarctic circle .

This is what the area is thought to have looked like. Dr Gess discovered 51 Devonian species which included africa’s earliest coelacanth and the world’s oldest lamprey. He also found many varieties of plant life both aquatic and land based.. The finds included the discovery of a scorpian, the earliest known land living animal from Gondwana, one of the two supercontinents that existed at that time.


John: I gues that makes us pretty unique?

Robb: absolutely, this site is completely unique , and collagues of mine ocme from all over the world to study these fossils from this site with us.

The fossils are stored in the Albany Museum in Grahamstown in a collection which provides more and more pieces to the puzzle of our evolution.

John: It must be an extraordinary feeling knowing that you are the first person to see something for the first time, to discover something for the first time.
Rob: Absolutely that’s a really special moment. And if you open a rock like this there is always the chance that there will be something there that no one has ever seen before.
John: Does it still excite you? Does it still rock your boat?
Rob: Oh it never loses its excitement and whats really exciting also about these rocks is that virtually everything that we have found in here, every type of thing that we have found in here, virtually every single one, has been new to science.

Dr. Gess has many international publications under his belt. He often addresses connferences overseas to discuss his work. It was he that SANRAL turned to provide the fossil component of the impact assessment report for a new road alignment which is now under construction 20km outside Grahamstown

Mpati: We undertook the environmental impact assesment and one of the findings was that alsmost like a red flag that there would be possible heritage finds in the area.

In that report Dr. Gess had pointed out something significant at coombs hill.

Rob: There was just a small layer there of a creamy white chalky rock which I recognized because I had worked at waterloo farm as weathered black shale.

And he was right. The site has revealed even more new secrets about our past.

John: Doc tell us about black shale and why it is important?
Rob: Well the black shale that we are looking at here formed as fine grained mud that settled in lagoon or estuaries and the reason that they are black is because they are so full of rotten plant matter. In fact they are so full of rotten plant matter that bacteria working on that used up all the oxygen in that mud and it formed what we call anoxic mud and in anoxic mud you can kind of pickle and preserve fossils extremely well.

Dr. Gess’s assistant Christopher Harris here is an uncovering a fossil from the black shale.

John: Chris what exactly have you uncovered here?
Chris: Well I have just found a matte of vegetation that has settled down onto the bottom of the lagoon floor. This is the first time that this has seen the sunlight in millions and millions of years so I feel quite lucky to have just opened this up.

Whilst both sites are unearthing fossils from the Devonian period, it’s thought the specimens are separated by millions of years.
Coombs Hill has so far yielded 10 Devonian species, which include two types of invertebrate, two types of seaweed and 6 types of land plant – only one of which was previously known. An astonishing discovery has been a completely intact frond of a tree called Archaeopteris notosaria, which had previously only been discovered as broken pieces at Waterloo in 1995.

Rob: We haven’t ever had such a beautiful one before and you can see each of these little leaflets coming off each of these twigs, it’s really exquisitely preserved.

This remarkable discovery is a world first. This local species of Archaeopteris notosaria belongs to the genus of cone bearing plants that gave rise to the first woody forests on earth

Sanral is now making provisions to make sure the public become aware of this historical site.

Mpati: It is actually great. Sanral ahs had to put together a plan as well on the road itself to allow for an observation area where tourists can stop and learn more about the heritage of the area.

A rest and picnic will be created. Information boards will be put up to show pictures of these fossils, as if snap shots from our past.

John: IT must be quite extraordinary doctor to look down at these fossils and to imagine that what you are looking at are photographs of this particular period of time.
Rob: So each of these snapshots is a snapshot of a piece of mud as it was just 1 day, 1 hour of 1 day 360 million years ago. Those little sticks were lying exactly as they are on this plane and a little bit of mud came and covered them and they slowly got buried.

LINK: So the question remains why should we care about something that is 360 million years old? Well at least part of the answer to that question is that it helps to unravel that great mystery about where exactly we come from?


South Africa continues to provide some of those answers. Because it has rare fossil histories from earliest life forms at Barberton to human ancestors at the cradle of mankind. Expect more discoveries from Dr. Gess and his team as they sift through rocks at the present site as well as thousands more from waterloo farm. He hopes that these discoveries will impact on young minds.

Rob: A lot of young people are very interested in science fiction and fantasy and this is in a way the other way around in that this is the discovery of actually facts about other worlds. They are other worlds; they were completely different from our world. The plants were different, the animals are very different so it’s whole other world but unlike science fiction this really existed and I think that’s really special.
